messages.author: d00f6178fa8e05fe
messages.subject: Mixture with Matt trick
parts:
Hi Stan,

I would like to know how would you implement mixture model for distributions after reparametrization with Matt trick?  For example in the simple model (except from that parameter z should be either from the x or y group distribution).

parameters {
  vector[9] y_raw;
  vector[9] x_raw;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[9] z;
  
  for (i in 1:9){
    z[i] <- 4 * y_raw;    // either from this distribution
    z[i] <- 10 + 2 * x_raw;   // or this one
  }
}
model {
  y_raw ~ normal(0,1);     // implies y ~ normal(0, 4)
  x_raw ~ normal(0,1);     // implies x ~ normal(10, 2)
}

Thanks,
Martin

Right, it would be like this:

parameters {
  vector[9] z;
}
model {
for (i in 1:9)

increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(.5) + normal_log(z, 0, 4),
                                                      log(.5) + normal_log(z, 10, 2))
}


Martin

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture with Matt trick
parts:
OK, I think I see what you're trying to do --- use
a normal mixture as a hierarchical prior.

To apply the Matt trick to a mixture prior, you have to
do the summation over the usage of the variable.

Suppose the total model is this, with lambda being the
mixture probability and mu and sigma the vectors of mixture
component parameters:

p(y,z,mu,sigma,lambda)
=
p(mu, sigma, lambda) // priors
* p(y | mu, sigma, lambda) // mixture for y
* p(z | y) // conditioning z on y

For example, with the suggested two-component normal mixture,
the density for y is:

p(y|mu,sigma,lambda)
= lambda * normal(y|mu[1],sigma[1]) + (1 - lambda) * normal(y|mu[2],sigma[2])

And suppose for concreteness that

p(z | y) = foo(z | y)

Then you can do the mixture with a non-centered (Matt tricked)
parameterization this way in Stan on the log scale:

parameters {
real y_raw;
}
model {
y_raw ~ normal(0,1);
increment_log_prob(
log_sum_exp(log(lambda) + foo_log(z, mu[1] + sigma[1] * y_raw),
log1m(lambda) + foo_log(z, mu[2] + sigma[2] * y_raw) ) );
... prior log p(lambda,mu,sigma) ...
}

This should work very well because y_raw should mix just fine compared
to trying to sample for y. I'm pretty sure I have this right, but it'd
be nice if someone else could check my logic here.

You don't get samples for y out, but you do get mu and sigma (as well
as lambda if you let that be a parameter instead of fixing at 0.5). You
could generate them in generated quantities as you did elsewhere.

- Bob

P.S. I also added a feature request for mixture functions on the log scale
to make writing mixture models a bit easier:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/970

That'd be:

log_mixture(real lambda, real lp1, real lp2)
= log_sum_exp(log(lambda) + lp1, log1m(lambda) + lp2)

where lambda must be in (0,1). And another more general version

log_mixture(vector theta, vector lp)
= log_sum_exp(log(theta) + lp)

where theta is a K-simplex and lp a K-vector.

> I actually want to use Matt trick in a hierarchical reinforcement-learning I brought up 2 weeks ago. Maybe you still remember, it's here: https://groups.google.com/forum/?hl=cs#!topic/stan-users/TjY3wQqUS2g
>
> I want to use Matt trick in the mixture part there. Would it be any use?

I'm not sure. One thing to think about is whether you
need separate normal(0,1) underlying raw parameters for
each of the mixture components. The suggestion I made a couple
days ago re-used the same one, but I'm not sure that's right
as it'll keep the multiple modes in lock step in the posterior.

The main reason to try it would be poor mixing of hierarchical
prior parameters.

> I tried to implement softmax as you suggested, but the performance didn't really improve.
>
> Since we're again talking about this model, you recommended us to use inv_logit instead of Phi, but it turned out that after this change model gives quite different posteriors for parameters of interest. Is Phi_approx also good choice here?

The parameters will be scaled differently with inv_logit and
Phi, but the effect should be roughly the same in terms of
regression predictions.

- Bob
